Chapter 3: Fighting for Equality in the Courts
By the time the 1970s rolled around, the world was really starting to change. The women’s movement was picking up steam, and the law was—finally—beginning to catch up. Ruth, now teaching law, saw a chance to make an impact—not just in the classroom, but in the courtroom too.
She teamed up with advocates who were challenging laws that treated men and women differently. Sometimes, those differences seemed tiny on paper, but they ended up having huge consequences in real life.
Take one case Ruth worked on—a widower who was denied Social Security benefits simply because the law assumed only women needed help when their spouse died. Sound fair? Ruth didn’t think so. She saw the real harm, and not just for women. Men, too, were boxed in by these old stereotypes.
So, Ruth crafted her arguments in a way that made judges stop and listen. She explained how gender discrimination hurts everyone—not just one side. And, she did it with this calm, logical style that stood out in court. No shouting, no grandstanding—just a steady voice and crystal-clear reasoning. She let the facts and the law speak for themselves.
Winning wasn’t easy. The legal system is notorious for being slow to change, and many judges were, let’s be honest, pretty skeptical. But Ruth was patient and strategic. She picked her cases carefully, aiming for ones that could set powerful precedents and slowly build a foundation for broader change.
Every win—no matter how small—chipped away at those old assumptions. And each one made it tougher for the law to keep ignoring the real lives and needs of people.
Outside the courtroom, Ruth was just as dedicated. She mentored students and young lawyers, always encouraging them to think deeply and see the law as something alive—something that could grow and change. She also balanced all this with family life, finding happiness in quiet moments with Marty and their kids. The demands were huge, but she handled them with the same careful discipline that got her through every challenge before.
As more people noticed her work, Ruth’s influence grew—not just because of her sharp legal mind, but because of her empathy. She had a rare ability to connect with folks from all walks of life. She knew that real change took more than just court wins; it needed cultural shifts too. So, she worked hard to build bridges between legal victories and everyday lives.
The fight for equality wasn’t over—not by a long shot. But Ruth had become one of its most effective champions. She proved that with persistence and smart strategy, even the toughest barriers could start to move.
